newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries, crushed by strong data, end lower.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries, crushed by strong data, end lower.

text.p: U.S. government securities, reeling under the blow dealt by strong U.S. economic data, kicked off 1997 the way they ended 1996 -- down.
The bellwether 30-year U.S. Treasury bond closed down 1-6/32 at 96-30/32, to yield 6.74 percent.
At the close on Tuesday, before the New Year holiday, the bond yielded 6.64 percent -- a level that itself reflected a selloff from the 5.54-percent yield registered on December 30.
Traders said the long bond's slump pushed the 30-year bond yield to 6.75-percent area -- a magnet for bargain hunters.

Traders reported buying interest from both domestic and foreign investors in the 6.75-percent long bond yield area -- confirming a December forecast by several Treasury market analysts that this level would attract bargain hunters.
One trader at a European brokerage firm on Wall Street said "at 6.75 percent, the long bond provides real value. It's coming back in line more or less with other major issuers."

The U.S. 30-year benchmark is now providing a return more in line with the 30-year German issue which yields 6.68 percent due to an inflation environment that is lower in Germany than in the United States.

The National Association of Purchasing Management Index rose to 54.0 in December from 52.7 in November. The index was well above the 50-percent reading that indicates manufacturing is expanding. It was also well above the 43.9-percent reading that divides expansion and recession.
Separately, the Conference Board reported its Help-Wanted Index shot up in November to 85 from 82 in October -- another confirmation the American consumer has spending power.
The NAPM and Help-Wanted reports led key players to speculate the Federal Reserve may not be as lenient on the interest rate front in 1997 as it was in 1996.
Also reported among the buyers of Treasuries were foreign central banks said to have put their buy orders in the two- to five-year note sector through the Fed.
Analyst John Canavan at Stone and McCarthy Research Associates admitted "the market ended 1996 on a very ugly note and began 1997 in the same vein."
"The overall NAPM index was well above expectations," Canavan noted. "That was bad enough but the NAPM price index component jumped quite sharply as well."
Canavan, however, pointed out Tresuries trim their losses toward the end of the session -- a sign of bottoming out.
Overall, the bearish mood that ushered in 1997 trading may not necessarily be a sign of things to come, traders said.
For one thing, volume was on the weak side.

GovPX, a real-time Treasury prices information service, said trading volume was about 7.0 percent below average for a Thursday in the first quarter and volume in the bill sector was 12 percent lighter than usual.

Also, David Resler, senior economist at Nomura Securities International, noted that, based on historical data, Treasury prices tend to be higher in January than in December in part because portfolio managers set up new positions.
Resler also said Treasury prices had a tendency to fall in the first week of trading in January -- without preventing gains for the entire month.
"In five out of the nine past years, the first week of trading showed weakness, but, for the month as a whole, (Treasury) prices have tended to be higher and yields lower," Resler pointed out.
One key factor for the Treasuries' outlook is the dollar's performance. Though pressured, the dollar has manged to uphold key support levels versus major currencies.
